Neonatal Tawny-breasted myiobius emerge from the egg after an incubation period of 15 days [ab = 15 days] when the nest is maintained at a steady temperature of 32 °C [T = 32 °C]. At the moment of hatching, these altricial nestlings are remarkably small, with a wet weight at birth of just 1.3 grams [Wwb = 1.3 grams]. This initial mass is modest even by tyrannid standards, reflecting the energy constraints imposed by producing a clutch in a challenging environment. The downy chicks are entirely dependent on biparental provisioning during the first days of life, and their developmental trajectory is tightly coupled to the thermal conditions within the domed nest structure.

Under the warmer thermal conditions that typically prevail during the active foraging period of the adults, measured at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the nestling period proceeds rapidly. Fledging, marked by the achievement of the first sustained flight, occurs at just 11 days after hatching [tx = 11 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This abbreviated nestling phase is characteristic of many small-bodied passerines that face high predation risk, and it necessitates a prodigious feeding effort from both parents to ensure the nestlings accumulate sufficient reserves for departure. The pin-feathered chicks grow visibly day by day, their metabolic machinery operating at a high rate to support feather development and somatic growth within this compressed developmental window.

Sexual maturation in this species follows a distinctly different timeline, with puberty estimated to occur at 33 days after hatching [tp = 33 days after hatching] under the same metabolic temperature regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This rapid progression to gonadal maturity is notable for a bird of this size, as many congeners delay reproductive activation for several additional weeks. The swift attainment of reproductive capability likely represents an adaptation to a seasonally fluctuating environment where breeding opportunities must be seized quickly. Following the completion of somatic growth, reproductively viable individuals begin to exhibit the characteristic plumage and breeding behaviors of sexually mature adults.

The first successful breeding event, however, is generally deferred considerably beyond the onset of puberty. Field records indicate that the time since birth at first brood is approximately 401.5 days [tR = approximately 401.5 days] when measured at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This delay between the achievement of sexual maturity and the initiation of reproduction suggests that young birds require a lengthy period to establish a territory, develop foraging proficiency, and undergo the physiological priming necessary to produce a clutch. The interval also reflects the constraints of a strongly seasonal environment where optimal nesting conditions may be limited to a narrow window each year.

Under the thermal conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the maximum reproductive output of female Tawny-breasted myiobius has been characterized through detailed field observations. Females typically produce two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch], and they are capable of raising one brood per year [F_R_i = one brood per year]. This modest annual reproductive effort is complemented by a relatively extended maximum lifespan of approximately 7.4 years [am = approximately 7.4 years], allowing for multiple breeding seasons over an individual's lifetime at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The ultimate wet weight for adult females reaches 14.1 grams [Wwi = 14.1 grams], a mass that supports the energetic demands of egg production and extended brooding. Basal oxygen consumption in resting adults was measured at 54.55 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 54.55 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value consistent with the elevated metabolic rate required to sustain the active insectivorous foraging strategy of this species at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C].
